title: Choose and order
summary: Select two or three supporting ideas that are relevant, developable and clearly linked, then arrange them in the order a reader needs.

sections.title: A pool is larger than a plan
content: E6.2 produced several possible I-S-A-R frames. A composition does not need to use all of them. Selection creates depth: two or three supporting ideas with specific actions and explanations are usually more useful than a long list of undeveloped points.

Keep the task contract visible. The original prompt still asks for one school-learned skill or idea. Your supporting ideas must develop that one focus rather than introduce a new school lesson each time.

sections.title: Apply the R-D-L test
content: Test each candidate three ways. Relevant means it answers the exact task contract. Developable means you can supply a situation, action and result or learning. Linked means you can explain how the evidence proves the value or transfer of the chosen school learning.

Keep candidates that pass all three tests. Repair one missing feature when the core idea is useful. Remove candidates that change the topic, repeat another point or need invented evidence to sound convincing.

sections.title: Select depth within one example
content: Focus: breaking a large task into smaller parts. Example: organising a school charity sale. Candidate one explains the planning action: divide publicity, supplies, prices and staffing, then give each part a deadline. Candidate two explains how the same method helped when rain forced the stalls indoors: identify urgent parts, reassign people and check what remained.

Both candidates are relevant, developable and linked. They deepen one example instead of merely naming two situations. A general claim that organisation is always useful adds little, while a paragraph about teamwork as a different school lesson would break the one-focus boundary.

sections.title: Combine overlap before ordering
content: If two candidates perform the same job, combine them. ‘I listed the sale tasks’ and ‘I separated the sale into four areas’ are one planning point, not two body ideas. Combining overlap leaves room to explain action, reasoning and result.
Give every selected idea a different job. One may establish how the method works, another may show it under pressure, and a final brief idea may explain the resulting lesson or a credible future use.

sections.title: Order by reader need
content: Ask what the reader must understand first, what evidence should follow and what insight becomes clear only after that evidence. For the charity-sale example, the reader needs the learned method before the initial plan, the initial plan before the unexpected rain, and both actions before the writer's reflection.

Useful relationships include chronological order for a changing event, cause and effect for explaining consequences, and simple to complex for explaining a method. Choose the relationship that makes the reasoning easiest to follow rather than placing the most dramatic detail first automatically.

sections.title: Diagnose weak selection and sequence
content: List planning keeps many shallow points. Focus switching changes the central school learning between paragraphs. Overlap treats repeated details as separate ideas. Evidence-before-context gives the reader a result or complication before explaining the situation needed to understand it.
Repair the plan by screening every candidate with R-D-L, combining overlap, assigning a distinct job to each selected idea and writing the order as a short arrow chain.

sections.title: Choose less and develop more
content: Use the E6.2 idea pool to make six selection and ordering decisions. Complete the group before viewing feedback, then carry the selected arrow chain into E6.4.
